subject: chemistry
title: Chemical Bonding & Structure Adventure 2: VSEPR shapes and intermolecular forces
welcome_lead: Today you'll predict molecular shapes with VSEPR — and feel intermolecular forces.
meta_desc: IBDP Chemistry — VSEPR, molecular shapes, London dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding.
final_note: You learned VSEPR predicts shapes from electron pair repulsion (linear, bent, trigonal, tetrahedral), and IMFs (London, dipole-dipole, H-bond) determine bp/mp.

concepts.def: H bonded to F, O, N

walkthroughs.body_html:
Count electron domains around central atom; repulsion pushes them apart.

- 2 domains → linear 180° (CO₂)
- 3 → trigonal planar 120° (BF₃)
- 4 → tetrahedral 109.5° (CH₄)
- 4 with 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal 107° (NH₃)
- 4 with 2 lone pairs → bent 104.5° (H₂O)
- 5 → trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅)
- 6 → octahedral (SF₆)

Lone pairs repel more than bond pairs.

Weakest to strongest:

- London dispersion — instantaneous dipoles; all molecules have them; stronger for larger Mr.
- Dipole-dipole — permanent dipoles attract (HCl, CO).
- Hydrogen bond — H attached to small electronegative F, O, N. Especially strong (~20-40 kJ/mol).

H₂O has bp 100°C — much higher than H₂S (-60°C) because H-bonds.

Ice less dense than water (open H-bond lattice) — floats!

DNA: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) hold the double helix.

Hybridisation: C in CH₄ is sp³; CH₂=CH₂ has sp²; CH≡CH has sp.
